paragraphs: Friend, here's what Psalm 74 teaches me: you can bring God the whole mess. Asaph, one of Israel's psalm writers, doesn't clean it up first. He asks, "Why have You rejected us forever, O God?" and he asks "How long?" and he tells God every ruined thing he can see. Nobody in this psalm gets told to calm down (Psalm 74:1, 10).

But watch the turn, because it's the whole point. Right in the middle of the hurt, Asaph says, "Yet God is my King from ancient times, working salvation on the earth." He doesn't stop being honest. He just stops looking only at the rubble and starts remembering who God has always been. The sea, the day and the night, the summer and winter all belong to Him (Psalm 74:12, 16, 17).

So when your own sanctuary feels burned down and nobody can tell you how long it'll last, do what Asaph did. Say it out loud, then say who your God is. He keeps asking God to remember His people, the afflicted, the poor and the needy, and that tells me God's ears are open to the ones at the bottom of the pile (Psalm 74:19, 21). Honest prayer and strong trust can sit in the same oven, baker, and this psalm bakes them together.
